name: The Russian Empire
title: Social Hierarchy of the Russian Empire: From Emperor to Serf
period: 1801–1861 (from the accession of Alexander I to the emancipation of the serfs)

tiers.name: The emperor
tiers.you: You rule as an autocrat, crowned in Moscow and sharing power with no assembly, but you must keep the landlords loyal and fear unrest among the serfs.
tiers.kid: The emperor, or tsar, ruled Russia alone, with no parliament to share his power.
tiers.rise: The throne passed to the emperor’s eldest son or, failing sons, to a brother: Alexander I left no son and was succeeded by his younger brother Nicholas I, after their brother Constantine had given up his claim.
tiers.why: The emperor was an autocrat: no assembly shared his power, and titles, ranks and privileges were his to grant.

tiers.name: Nobles
tiers.you: You own an estate and the serfs who work it, pay no poll tax and cannot be flogged, and you need not serve, though you probably spend some years as an officer; your estate may well be mortgaged.
tiers.kid: Many nobles owned large country estates and the serfs who farmed them.
tiers.rise: Nobility came by birth, by imperial grant, or by rising through the Table of Ranks: Mikhail Speransky, a village priest’s son, rose through the civil service to become Alexander I’s leading adviser and was made a count in 1839.
tiers.why: The nobility (dvoryanstvo) was the first estate.

tiers.name: Orthodox clergy
tiers.term: beloe dukhovenstvo (white clergy), chernoe dukhovenstvo (black clergy)
tiers.you: You are a priest’s son and a priest yourself, married before your ordination; you pay no poll tax and cannot be taken as a recruit, but your parish is poor and you live much like your parishioners.
tiers.kid: Orthodox parish priests could marry, and their sons were expected to become priests too.
tiers.rise: Priests’ sons usually followed their fathers, but the seminaries also fed the civil service: Mikhail Speransky, a village priest’s son, taught at the seminary in Saint Petersburg before entering state service and rising to the top.
tiers.why: The Orthodox clergy was the second estate free of the poll tax and of the recruit levy, but it was divided.

tiers.name: Merchants
tiers.you: You have declared your capital and enrolled in a merchant guild, and your business may grow rich, but the nobles look down on you and you have no say in how the empire is ruled.
tiers.kid: Merchants were traders who paid to join a merchant guild, which gave them the right to trade.
tiers.rise: Anyone who could declare enough capital and pay the fees could enrol in a guild, and some merchants began as townspeople or even serfs: Savva Morozov, a serf, bought freedom for himself and his sons in 1820, and the family went on to found the Morozov textile companies.
tiers.why: The merchants (kupechestvo) were enrolled in three guilds according to the capital they declared, under Catherine II’s rules of 1775, each guild with its own trading rights.

tiers.name: Townspeople
tiers.you: You are registered in your town as one of its meshchane, keep a small shop or work at a craft, pay the poll tax and may be taken as a recruit.
tiers.kid: Townspeople ran small shops and workshops in Russia’s towns and paid taxes to the government.
tiers.rise: A townsman who gathered enough capital could enrol as a merchant, and peasants allowed to settle in a town could join the meshchane if they owned property and worked there.
tiers.why: The meshchane were the lower urban estate, ranked above the peasants and below the merchant guilds: small traders, artisans, shopkeepers and urban workers who were registered in a town but could not meet the merchants’…

tiers.name: Cossacks
tiers.you: You hold land free of taxes in your Cossack village, and in return you serve for years in your host’s regiments with your own horse and equipment.
tiers.kid: Cossacks were horsemen of the frontier who were given land in return for serving in the army.
tiers.rise: Cossack status passed from father to son, and the officers of the hosts could be admitted to the nobility.
tiers.why: The Cossacks, once free frontier communities of runaway serfs, adventurers and steppe warriors, had become a hereditary military estate of the empire by the end of the 18th century.

tiers.name: Soldiers
tiers.you: You were chosen as a recruit by your village or your master and serve for twenty years or more, far from home; if you survive, you will come home a free man.
tiers.kid: Russian soldiers were taken from their villages and served in the army for many years.
tiers.rise: A few soldiers of humble birth rose to officer’s rank, which brought nobility under the Table of Ranks.
tiers.why: The army’s rank and file were recruits drawn from the estates that paid the poll tax, above all the peasants.

tiers.name: State and crown peasants
tiers.you: You farm your commune’s share of state land, pay the poll tax and your quit-rent to the treasury and send recruits to the army; no one can sell you, but you cannot move away freely.
tiers.kid: State peasants farmed land that belonged to the government, and unlike serfs they could not be sold.
tiers.rise: A state peasant who prospered could buy land and could leave for a town or a merchant guild if he met their requirements; in the 18th century, however, the crown had given hundreds of thousands of state peasants to nobles as serfs.
tiers.why: About as many peasants lived on the land of the state as on private estates.

tiers.name: Serfs
tiers.you: You work your lord’s fields three days a week or pay him a quit-rent, and he can punish you, sell you, send you to the army and must approve your marriage.
tiers.kid: Serfs were farmers who belonged to a landowner and were not allowed to leave his estate.
tiers.rise: A serf could be freed by his master, buy his freedom if the master agreed, or leave serfdom as a recruit. From 1803 lords could free whole villages as “free agriculturalists”, but by 1858 only about 152,000 male serfs, 1.5 per cent, had been freed that way.
tiers.why: Serfs were peasants owned, with the land they lived on, by noble landlords, and bound to it since the Law Code of 1649.

tiers.name: Household serfs
tiers.you: You live in your master’s house as a cook, a groom or a maid, with no land of your own; he can sell you on your own, and his favour or cruelty rules your life.
tiers.kid: Household serfs worked as servants in a landowner’s house and had no land of their own.
tiers.rise: Freedom came by an owner’s grace or by purchase: Count Nikolai Sheremetev freed Praskovia Zhemchugova in 1798 and married her in secret in 1801.
tiers.why: Beside the field serfs lived the household serfs (dvorovye), who had no land and served in their master’s house and stables as cooks, coachmen, grooms, maids, footmen, nurses and stewards.
